Article Title: Govt dissolves digital communications commission with immediate effect
Article Text:
Govt has dissolved its apex decision-making body for telecom and digital communication. (Representative image)

NEW DELHI: Governmnet has with immediate effect dissolved its apex decision-making body for telecom and digital communication — digital communications commission (DCC), which was originally established as telecom commission in 1989 before being renamed in 2018.The communication ministry’s dept of telecommunications notified this decision through a Sept 19, 2026, resolution that was published in the Gazette of India, Monday “with effect from the date of publication of this resolution, the DCC shall stand dissolved,” says the gazette.Decisions for projects upto Rs 100 crore can be taken by the secretary DoT, upto Rs 500 crore by the telecom minister and those above Rs 500 crore to Rs 1,000 were considered by the DCC. Now the same will be referred to the expenditure finance committee, inter-ministerial body under finmin’s dept of expenditure which will evaluate the same before being submitted to the cabinet for formal approval.“The decision was notified last week. DCCA used to have chairman (secretary DoT) and three members. Now that structure will be replaced by an advisor in the ministry. Those changes are being made,” said people aware of the matter.The gazette dissolving DCC traces its history. It was set up as telecom commission in April 1989 to “deal with various aspects relating to the telecommunications sector.” It was re-designated as DCC in October 2018.
Article Summary: Govt has dissolved its apex decision-making body for telecom and digital communication. Digital communications commission (DCC) was originally established as telecom commission in 1989. Decisions for projects upto Rs 100 crore can be taken by the secretary DoT. Those above Rs 500 crore to Rs 1,000 were considered by DCC.

Article Title: ‘Travel to Coimbatore, Madurai’: Annamalai takes swipe at Vijay’s UK trip

NEW DELHI: Former Tamil Nadu BJP president criticised chief minister and TVK leader C Joseph Vijay’s recent visit to London to attract investments, arguing that the state government should instead focus on encouraging local industries to expand and invest.“Chief Minister Mr. Vijay has returned from London after attracting investments. The growth of the United Kingdom is only 1%. The investments there are being made by our Indian companies, including Mahindra,” he said.He added, “Therefore, instead of the Chief Minister traveling abroad, incentives should be provided to our industrial companies in cities including Coimbatore and Madurai, and they should be encouraged to make investments.”The remarks come as DMK president MK Stalin also criticised Vijay’s recent London visit, questioning what investments the Chief Minister had secured for Tamil Nadu during the trip.Addressing the annual Mupperum Vizha at Kalaignar Arangam at the DMK headquarters, Stalin said, “CM Sir, why did you go to London? What investments have you brought to Tamil Nadu? Why do you have to go to London and sign agreements with an Indian company?”Taking an apparent swipe at Vijay, Stalin added, “He had earlier stated that he would no longer act in films, but he continues to perform before the public.Earlier there was local shooting; now there is foreign shooting.”Vijay concluded his six-day official visit to the United Kingdom last week, securing investment commitments worth Rs 15,300 crore that are expected to generate more than 10,000 direct and indirect jobs in Tamil Nadu.The visit is part of the state’s strategic roadmap to transform Tamil Nadu into a USD 1.5 trillion economy by 2036 through transparent and efficient governance, according to an official release.During his visit, CM Vijay met Indian High Commissioner to the UK Kumaran Periasamy on September 12 to discuss trade opportunities arising from the India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA).On September 14, MoUs and Letters of Intent were formalised across auto components, R&D, renewable energy, power grid equipment and Global Capability Centres (GCCs).
Article Summary: Vijay concluded his six-day official visit to the UK last week, securing investment commitments worth Rs 15,300 crore. DMK president MK Stalin also criticised Vijay’s recent London visit, questioning what investments the Chief Minister had secured for Tamil Nadu.

NEW DELHI: Congress on Monday targeted Prime Minister Narendra Modi-led central government over "skyrocketing prices" of food and other commodities, using the popular Bollywood song "Kya hua tera vada" to question the PM's silence on inflation.Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh shared a media report on rising prices of food items, pulses and cooking oil, and alleged that the increase was putting pressure on household budgets."The skyrocketing prices of food items in the country have broken the back of the middle and poor classes," Ramesh said in a post in Hindi. He said rising prices were making pulses and other essential food items increasingly difficult for poorer households to afford."But the Prime Minister remains silent on inflation. The country is asking, 'Where have the 'achche din' gone, Prime Minister ji?' Are they only left in sermons?" he said."The people go hungry, the government stays silent," Ramesh said, questioning whether this was the "new India".Taking a swipe at the government, Ramesh wrote, "Kya hua tera vada? Woh kasam, woh irada?", a reference to the popular song from the 1977 Bollywood film Hum Kisise Kum Nahin.Ramesh claimed that prices of several everyday commodities had risen sharply in recent months, adding to the burden on households."In the past month, spice prices have surged by a massive 10% to 25%. Green cardamom has risen from 4000 rupees to 4400 rupees/kg, black cardamom from 2400 rupees to 2800 rupees/kg, and cumin has jumped from 360 rupees to 400 rupees/kg. Mace prices have shot up directly from 2500 rupees to 3000 rupees per kg,” Jairam said."Arhar dal has increased from 100 rupees to 130 rupees/kg, chana dal from 70 rupees to 100 rupees/kg, and urad from 120 rupees to 140 rupees/kg. Mustard oil has reached 210 rupees/litre from 190 rupees, and Safola oil has climbed to 280 rupees/litre from 240 rupees," he added.Ramesh also claimed that onion prices had risen sharply between June and September. “From June to September, the all-India average retail price of onions rose from 29.50 rupees/kg to 53.78 rupees/kg - a staggering 82.3% increase in just three and a half months," he said.The Congress leader called on the Modi government to take immediate measures to address what he described as "uncontrolled inflation" and provide relief to consumers.

He said rising prices were making pulses and other essential food items increasingly difficult for poorer households to afford. Article Title: Bengal SIR tribunals may take 12 years to decide on appeals
Article Text:
SIR appeals pile up in WB, EC says hike number of tribunals

Excessive backlog

Poll Vote & Share your view What should be the priority for resolving voter-list appeals? Faster disposal of appeals More appellate tribunals Better accessibility for voters Greater transparency in the process 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: The innumerable voters in West Bengal who were removed from the electoral rolls after special intensive revision (SIR) may not be able to vote for more than a decade as appellate tribunals set up by Supreme Court could take more than 12 years to decide on their appeals for inclusion, going by the present pace of adjudication.An affidavit filed by Election Commission before Supreme Court says 1,26,194 applications have been decided by tribunals in the last five months since they started functioning in mid-April. So, on average, 25,238 cases are being decided by the tribunals in a month when even Saturdays and Sundays are included as working days. The total number of pending cases as of Sept 16, when the affidavit was filed, was 37,05,235. At current speed, if the tribunals work seven days a week, it would take 146 months to decide all cases.Admitting that the present infrastructure and number of tribunals are insufficient to handle the Herculean task of adjudicating 37 lakh cases, the poll panel pleaded with the court to increase the number of tribunals in the state from 24 to 42, almost double the present strength, and allow judicial officers to work from home."With a view to further streamlining and expediting the disposal of the pending appeals, it is proposed that the number of appellate tribunals in the state of West Bengal may be considered for increase to correspond with the number of parliamentary constituencies in the state, so as to facilitate expeditious disposal of the pending appeals," said the affidavit, filed in response to a petition from TMC MP Derek O' Brien. Allowing judicial workers to conduct hearings and undertake other proceedings from home "would assist in expediting the disposal of pending appeals by minimising the time lost in conveyance", it said.In another affidavit filed in response to a petition on the functioning of the tribunals, the commission said they were constituted pursuant to the directives of the apex court and the standard operating procedure (SOP) governing their functioning has been formulated by the committee constituted for this purpose, comprising, inter alia, former judges of the high court at Calcutta."It is humbly submitted that the reliefs sought by the petitioner pertain primarily to the functioning, procedure and accessibility of the appellate mechanism and, therefore, fall within the domain of the SOP governing the functioning of the appellate tribunals and the authorities entrusted with the administration thereof. The feasibility, modalities and implementation... are matters best left to the consideration of the concerned appellate tribunal. .." the affidavit said.
Article Summary: EC says 1,26,194 applications have been decided by tribunals in the last five months since they started functioning in mid-April. On average, 25,238 cases are being decided in a month when even Saturdays and Sundays are included as working days. Total number of pending cases as of Sept 16, when the affidavit was filed, was 37,05,235. At current speed, if the tribunal work seven days a week, it would take 146 months to decide all cases.

Article Title: Amit Shah wants UCC in all NDA states by 2029. What will JD(U) do in Bihar?
Article Text:
What is UCC

BJP's old promise

Why UCC needs careful balancing for JD(U)

When JD(U) differed with BJP

Mahagathbandhan's offer to Nitish

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Is the implementation of the Uniform Civil Code emerging as a new point of contention between the Bharatiya Janata Party and one of its oldest allies, Janata Dal (United)?The question has come into focus after Union home minister Amit Shah's assertion that UCC would be implemented in all 21 NDA-ruled states before the next Lok Sabha elections prompted differing reactions within the JD(U).The issue surfaced after Shah, during his visit to Mumbai, put a timeline on BJP's plan to implement one of its longstanding ideological objectives before the 2029 Lok Sabha polls."Triple talaq has been abolished, giving Muslim women equal rights. We have introduced the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in several states and I am confident that in the 21 BJP-NDA ruled states, we will introduce the UCC before 2029," Shah said.Shah's message, however, drew a different response from some JD(U) leaders in Bihar.JD(U) general secretary and former minister Shyam Rajak said his party did not favour implementing UCC in the state."Our stand on the issue was made clear by our leader way back. He had said that although our party was supporting the UCC Bill in the Parliament, it was not in favour of implementing the same in Bihar," Rajak said."The chief minister may be of the BJP but the government is being run with the help of allies...our stand is clear, the question of implementing UCC in Bihar does not arise," he added.However, Bihar deputy chief minister Vijay Kumar Chaudhary, who is considered to be a close ally of former chief minister Nitish Kumar, adopted a more cautious stance and said the party would first study the legislation and would not oppose it "for no reason" if its provisions were found to be unexceptionable."As of now, we are not aware of the details of the legislation on UCC. Let it be placed before us. If we find there is nothing objectionable, why shall we oppose it without any reason? And if there are points of concern, these will be conveyed to the Union home minister," Chaudhary said.JD(U) working president Sanjay Jha has also indicated that party leaders would discuss the issue with Shah.For now, therefore, JD(U)'s stand is not entirely clear. While some leaders have spoken against implementing UCC in Bihar, remarks by senior leaders such as Chaudhary and Jha have left scope for the party to examine the proposed provisions before taking a final position. The party has historically favoured wider consultations and consensus on the issue.India already has uniform criminal laws and common civil laws covering matters such as taxation, contracts and negotiable instruments. However, when it comes to personal laws such as marriage, divorce and inheritance of property, different religious communities follow laws based on their respective traditions and practices.Article 44 under the Directive Principles of State Policy of the Constitution says that the State shall endeavour to secure a UCC for citizens throughout India."The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India," the Constitution says.A UCC broadly seeks to provide a common legal framework for citizens in matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance and succession.The Uniform Civil Code has been a longstanding part of the BJP's political agenda and has featured repeatedly in the party's election manifestos over the years.The party has repeatedly included the issue in its election manifestos, arguing that a common civil code would ensure equality before law and strengthen women's rights in matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption.Matters such as marriage, divorce, adoption, wills, intestacy and succession fall in the Concurrent List, allowing both the Centre and state governments to make laws on them.In 2022, then Union law minister Kiren Rijiju also informed the Rajya Sabha that states were empowered to legislate on these subjects."Article 44 of the Constitution provides that the State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India," Rijiju had said in a written reply."Personal laws such as intestacy and succession; wills; joint family and partition; marriage and divorce, relate to Entry 5 of List-III-Concurrent List of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, and hence, the States are also empowered to legislate upon them," he had added.This has allowed BJP-ruled states to take the state route on UCC.Uttarakhand became the first state in independent India to implement a state-specific Uniform Civil Code on January 27, 2025.Since then, UCC Bills have also been passed by the assemblies of BJP-ruled Gujarat, Assam and Madhya Pradesh. As of mid-September, the Bills in these three states were awaiting the President's assent.Other NDA-ruled states are at different stages of considering or preparing their own legislation.Shah's latest remarks have now put a 2029 timeline on that process for all NDA-ruled states.For JD(U), the issue comes with both political and ideological considerations.Nitish Kumar has long maintained that a reform such as UCC should not be pushed without broad consultation and consensus, particularly given India's social and religious diversity.There is also an electoral dimension.Within the NDA in Bihar, JD(U) has traditionally sought support across a social coalition that includes Extremely Backward Classes, women and sections of minorities. While its support among Muslims has weakened over the years, the party has continued to reach out to the community.Muslims constitute around 17.7% of Bihar's population, according to the state's caste survey. Recent electoral data cited by The Indian Express suggests that only a relatively small section of Muslim voters backed the NDA in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, underlining the challenge for JD(U) in retaining support among the community while remaining part of the BJP-led alliance.In the 2025 assembly election, JD(U) fielded four Muslim candidates, but only Mohammad Zama Khan won from the Chainpur seat.The political setting has also changed since that election.The NDA won 202 of Bihar's 243 assembly seats, with the BJP emerging as the single-largest party with 89 seats and JD(U) winning 85.Nitish Kumar is also no longer chief minister, with BJP's Samrat Choudhary now heading the NDA government. JD(U), however, remains one of its two principal constituents.This makes the UCC question an important one for the alliance: BJP has put a timeline on a longstanding policy commitment, while JD(U) has traditionally stressed consultation before any such move.Although an ally of BJP, JD(U) has not always agreed with it on politically sensitive issues.On UCC itself, Nitish Kumar has long cautioned against hurried implementation.In January 2017, as Bihar chief minister, he returned the Law Commission's questionnaire on UCC, arguing that there was insufficient clarity about what the proposed code would contain and calling for wider consultations with affected groups.Nitish argued that diverse customs and practices had existed for centuries and that any effort towards a common code should be based on consensus rather than simply imposed.JD(U) has also differed from the BJP on issues such as the Triple Talaq Bill and the abrogation of Article 370.In 2019, JD(U) opposed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Bill, commonly known as the Triple Talaq Bill. The party objected particularly to the provision making instant triple talaq a criminal offence, arguing that the legislation could create "a lack of trust" in society. Its MPs walked out of the Lok Sabha debate and later abstained during the Rajya Sabha proceedings.In August 2019, the party also opposed the Modi government's decision to abrogate the special status of Jammu and Kashmir under Article 370 and reorganise the former state into two Union Territories. JD(U) MPs staged a walkout when the measures were introduced in Parliament.However, it struck a reconciliatory note later and said that once the law had come into force, it should be abided by all.These differences did not, by themselves, prevent the BJP and JD(U) from working together. The two allies have in the past maintained separate positions on some issues while continuing their political partnership.UCC could similarly depend on what form a proposed law for Bihar eventually takes and whether the allies are able to arrive at a common position.Amid the debate over UCC, Congress and Rashtriya Janata Dal have taken the opportunity to invite Nitish Kumar to join the opposition alliance.RJD MLA Bhai Virendra asked Nitish to break ties with the BJP and form a new government with its support, saying the parties shared a socialist political tradition.The RJD MLA alleged that Nitish was surrounded by people who were "hellbent on ruining his political career" and said, "We urge Nitish Kumar ji to walk out of the NDA and form a govt with our support."Former Bihar Congress president and Rajya Sabha member Akhilesh Prasad Singh also extended an invitation to Nitish to join the Mahagathbandhan, saying Nitish had long been associated with socialist politics."It is the agenda of the BJP and the RSS. Several allies of the NDA may not agree with it, and Nitish certainly should not agree with it. He has always been associated with social concerns and socialism, so I do not think he can ever agree with this," Singh said."Why would Congress have any objection to that? If he leaves, Congress will always welcome him," he added.For now, however, the differing remarks on UCC do not necessarily point to a larger crisis within the Bihar NDA.JD(U)'s final position remains open. Some of its leaders have opposed implementation in Bihar, while others have said the party should first see the proposed legislation and discuss its concerns with the BJP leadership.Shah, meanwhile, has set a clear target of introducing UCC in all NDA-ruled states before 2029.It remains to be seen whether Bihar eventually follows that roadmap and, if it does, what shape the proposed law takes after consultations between the two allies.
Article Summary: Union home minister Amit Shah's assertion that UCC would be implemented in all 21 NDA-ruled states prompted differing reactions within the JD(U) The issue surfaced after Shah put a timeline on BJP's plan to implement one of its longstanding ideological objectives before the 2029 Lok Sabha polls.

Article Title: India to make 350 kmph bullet trains by 2030, match Japan's E10
Article Text:
The current cost of the project works out to around Rs 399 crore per km

NEW DELHI: India will manufacture indigenous high-speed or bullet trains with a design speed of 350 kmph (B35) by 2030, matching Japan's next-generation E10 series trains that are scheduled for production the same year, according to the railway ministry's Cabinet proposal seeking approval for the revised cost of the Mumbai-Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail (MAHSR) project.Cabinet has approved the revised cost of the project at over Rs 2 lakh crore, nearly double the original estimate prepared in 2015, and the expenditure of nearly Rs 1 lakh crore escalated cost will come from budgetary support.TOI has learnt that the ministry informed the Cabinet it has initiated the process to develop B35 trains after the Japanese side conveyed in Dec 2024 that production of existing E5 series trains was being phased out. It mentions that Japan indicated that production of E10 trains would begin in 2030 and they would be ready for operations by 2034. Officials said deployment of E10 trains would be explored when they become available.The ministry has said that manufacturing of indigenous B28 high-speed trains has been taken up and India will also develop its own Bharat Train Control System (BTCS). The move mirrors China's indigenous CTCS signalling and train control system, which manages speed, spacing and safety across conventional and high-speed rail networks.As per the ministry, sharp increase in project cost from earlier Rs 1.1 lakh crore is largely due to a more than three-fold rise in land acquisition cost to about Rs 19,700 crore; a nearly 50% increase in infrastructure cost to over Rs 1 lakh crore, and around 100% escalation in spending on trains and signalling systems compared with the 2015 estimate.The current cost of the project, excluding future Japanese trains, works out to around Rs 399 crore per km.Initially, the Mumbai-Ahmedabad corridor will operate with B28 trains having a design speed of 280 kmph, while their maximum operating speed will be "249 kmph". BEML has received contracts to manufacture 32 B28 trains.Two prototype trains are expected to be ready for trial runs in the first quarter of 2027. BEML informed the BSE on Friday that it has received a separate Rs 5,400-crore contract to manufacture 15 additional B28 trains. The full 508-km Mumbai-Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail corridor is targeted for completion by Dec 2030.
Article Summary: India will manufacture indigenous high-speed or bullet trains with a design speed of 350 kmph (B35) The railway ministry's Cabinet proposal seeking approval for the revised cost of the Mumbai-Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail (MAHSR) project. Cabinet has approved revised cost at over Rs 2 lakh crore, nearly double original estimate.

Article Title: Using recovery agents proves costly for truck financier, SC orders Rs 15 lakh payout
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Criticising the use of muscle power by financiers to get back hypothecated vehicles, Supreme Court has told one of them to pay Rs 15 lakh to a truck owner who had taken a loan of Rs 10.4 lakh to buy the vehicle.Nearly two years after sanctioning the loan in June 2021, Cholamandalam Investment and Finance stealthily took back the truck over default in payment of EMIs. CCTV footage of a godown in Ayodhya on April 9, 2023, showed four persons breaking the vehicle's steering lock around 1am and driving it away. Six months later, Cholamandalam sent a notice saying it had taken back the vehicle and auctioned it for Rs 4.5 lakh, and the balance amount of Rs 1.3 lakh was still to be paid by him.A Supreme Court bench of Justices P S Narasimha and Alok Aradhe said though repossession of a hypothecated vehicle was a valid step to securitise the asset financed, it had to be done legally, with the procedure conforming to RBI's guidelines on Fair Practices Code for Lenders issued on May 5, 2003.
Article Summary: Cholamandalam Investment and Finance stealthily took back the truck over default in payment of EMIs. CCTV footage of a godown in Ayodhya on April 9, 2023, showed four persons breaking the vehicle's steering lock around 1am and driving it away.

NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu minister A Rajmohan on Sunday defended the state government’s decision to build a new assembly-cum-secretariat complex, saying "severe space constraints" at the existing premises have made an alternative necessary.“The space constraints at the current premises are genuine. The facility is planned to include modern amenities and house both the legislative assembly and the secretariat.

Digital healthcare cannot mean digital-only healthcare

What if your phone becomes the first thing you need to see a doctor?As healthcare increasingly moves from hospital counters and paper records to apps and online portals, access to care is becoming closely tied to access to technology.For many patients, digital healthcare can mean quicker consultations, easier access to medical records and fewer trips to hospitals. But for others, particularly older people, rural communities, low-income families and those with limited digital literacy, the shift can add another layer of difficulty.The problem is not simply whether a person owns a smartphone. Patients may struggle with internet connectivity, downloading and navigating apps, remembering passwords and OTPs, uploading documents or understanding information presented online.In many households, a single smartphone is shared by several family members, while caregivers often become the bridge between patients and digital health services.As government and private healthcare services increasingly encourage, and in some cases require, people to use digital platforms, a larger question is emerging: Is technology making healthcare more accessible, or creating a new barrier to accessing it?Digital health has opened up several ways for patients to manage their care remotely.People can consult doctors online, monitor blood sugar through connected devices, receive medication and appointment reminders, and access diet and educational resources without making frequent hospital visits.Telemedicine became particularly important during the Covid-19 pandemic, when lockdowns made physical consultations difficult. But the experience also exposed how uneven access to digital healthcare could be.A DIG-EQUITY study published in, examining the experiences of people with diabetes, caregivers, healthcare providers, policymakers and community organisations in urban and rural Tamil Nadu, found significant differences in how people used digital health services.Younger patients were generally more comfortable with smartphones, health applications and teleconsultations, while many older people needed family members to book appointments, join consultations or access medical reports.For some, physical limitations added to the problem. Impaired vision or hearing, as well as difficulty handling smartphones, could make navigating digital platforms harder.Even among younger people, digital access did not automatically translate into a preference for online care. Some people with type 1 diabetes continued to prefer in-person consultations because of the need for physical examinations.The digital divide is also closely linked to where people live and what they can afford.Urban patients are more likely to have reliable internet connections, smartphones and access to digital services. A study published in, examining barriers to digital health transformation in India, found that the challenges went beyond simply having a smartphone or internet connection.The study identified poor network coverage and inadequate IT infrastructure, the high cost of devices and digital systems, a lack of technical expertise, language and communication barriers, and difficulties faced by users among the major challenges.For patients, these barriers can have very practical consequences. The study noted that some had to rely on family members' smartphones to attend teleconsultations, while the cost of smart devices could limit access to mobile health applications.The findings suggest that digital access cannot be measured simply by whether someone owns a phone. Reliable connectivity, affordability, digital skills, language accessibility and the availability of human support all influence whether a patient can actually use digital healthcare.That distinction becomes particularly important as healthcare services increasingly move online. Putting a service on a digital platform does not automatically make it accessible to everyone.India's digital health infrastructure is expanding rapidly. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), through platforms such as ABHA, is aimed at creating a connected digital health ecosystem, while eSanjeevani has widened access to telemedicine.With hundreds of millions of ABHA IDs created and telemedicine consultations running into hundreds of millions, the scale of this shift is significant.But the benefits of digital healthcare are not evenly experienced.The gap becomes particularly visible when digital systems are introduced at the hospital level. For some patients, the shift has not removed queues; it has created an additional one.Rekha (name changed), a patient at the Delhi National Cancer Institute, said patients earlier had to wait in a single OPD queue, with doctors arriving around 8am. According to her, the process now involves generating a token through the ABHA app before reaching the hospital, followed by another number at the reception.“Earlier there used to be only one OPD line and the doctors used to arrive at 8am. Now they have made it mandatory to download the ABHA app and apply for a token number. Then we get another number from reception, and doctors arrive at 10am. Several patients need immediate care, but this extra queue has made life a bit more difficult,” she said.For those without a smartphone or reliable internet connection, Rekha said the process can begin hours before they reach the doctor. Some patients, she said, arrive around midnight or 1am and spend the night waiting because they cannot access the network or generate a digital token.Those with smartphones may apply through the ABHA app around 5am and reach the hospital by 7am, she said, only to wait again at reception before seeing a doctor later in the morning.Dr Manisha Arora, Director, Internal Medicine, CK Birla Hospital, Delhi, said ABHA should remain a facilitator rather than become a gateway to treatment.“A patient should never feel that access to technology determines access to healthcare,” she said, noting that patients without an ABHA ID, smartphone or internet connectivity should continue to be able to register physically and receive the same clinical care.She stressed that hospitals should adopt a digital-first, not digital-only, approach.“That means retaining manual registration counters, providing assisted kiosks and having dedicated digital-support personnel, particularly for elderly and first-time users.”Digital insurance processes are another area where patients can struggle. Families dealing with hospitalisation may simultaneously have to navigate e-KYC, pre-authorisation, co-payments, deductions and non-payable items.Manivannan Selvaraj, Founder and Managing Director, Kauvery Group of Hospitals, said translating a clinical treatment plan into a pre-authorisation submission, and then managing the queries and follow-ups that come back, involves a long chain of steps that a patient is neither equipped nor educated to handle, and should not have to handle while they or a family member is unwell.“Sometimes delays or claim issues arise because documentation is incomplete rather than because of a medical concern,” Arora said, stressing that hospital insurance desks need to act as patient counsellors, explaining the process rather than merely uploading documents.“True digital accessibility is when technology works in the background and the patient still experiences a human interface at the front,” she said.At 65, Amarnath (name changed) has an insurance policy but says managing it digitally has become difficult. He is often unsure about when he can claim, when premiums are due and how to complete the process online, leaving his son to handle the details for him.“I have an insurance policy, but I often don’t know when I can make a claim, when the premium is due or how to complete these processes online. My son manages it for me. At my age, it is not always easy to visit a centre every time I need to check my policy or make a claim. If healthcare is becoming digital, these services should also be made accessible to elderly people, so that we can manage them ourselves without having to depend on others,” he said.He also highlighted how the growing use of digital payments in hospitals can create another challenge for elderly patients unfamiliar with the technology. Having a UPI-enabled phone does not necessarily mean being comfortable using it, particularly during a medical emergency when payments may need to be made quickly.“I have UPI on my phone, but for people of our generation, it is difficult to become fully comfortable with the process and make an immediate payment, especially during a health emergency. This is something that should also be addressed,” he said.The pandemic offered an early and stark example of how closely technology and healthcare had become intertwined.While telemedicine and digital systems helped patients access services during lockdowns, other parts of the healthcare chain showed that digitisation alone could not solve problems of capacity and access.As reported byearlier, delays in Covid testing became a major concern during the second wave. Udham Singh, 22, developed high fever, severe cough, body ache and breathlessness after his sample was collected for an RT-PCR test. His report, which confirmed Covid infection, came several days after the sample was taken.“I would have landed in an ICU had I waited for some more time. The element of uncertainty due to delay also caused extreme mental trauma,” Singh said.For patients waiting at home, the delay was not merely an inconvenience. It affected decisions about treatment and isolation. Some families also faced difficulties maintaining quarantine while waiting for test results.Priya Jaiswal, a resident of Old Delhi, recalled how a network outage during the pandemic left her dependent on officials for essential medicines. With her internet connection down, she could not use UPI to make payments or order medicines online, leaving her waiting for officials to arrive at her home.“We had to wait for hours for officials to arrive and hand over the medicines while we were in quarantine. Even online consultations became difficult because of continuous power cuts at a time when we needed healthcare the most,” she said.The surge in demand for Covid testing also put pressure on government laboratories to issue digital reports on time, highlighting another challenge for digital healthcare: a digital interface is only as effective as the system supporting it.Covid-19 vaccination certificates also affected people's travel and employment plans.Varghese Thomas, a youth from the city, told TOI that five people in his group had taken their first vaccine dose around the same time, but only one had received the certificate nearly 40 days later.“When we applied for jobs, prospective employers were asking us about the vaccination. They wanted us to produce the certificate,” he said.Registering through Co-WIN was another difficulty for people in rural areas.As reported byearlier, 68-year-old Adhi Kesavan from Gudiyattam in Tamil Nadu's Vellore district had to travel around 5-7 km with his wife to a common service centre to register for vaccination.Kesavan did not own a smartphone or know how to use one. He was directed to the centre by his panchayat head, who told him that his details could be registered there and that the hospital would contact him when a vaccine became available.“I heard from our panchayat head that we can get vaccinated if we register at the e-sevai maiyyam. Our number will be given to the hospitals nearby and we will get a call once the vaccine is ready,” Kesavan said.He was still waiting for that call.India's digital-health expansion will ultimately be measured not only by how many people are connected to the system, but also by whether those who are not can still access care with the same ease and dignity.The goal should not be to make healthcare digital at any cost. It should be to make healthcare more accessible, using technology when it helps, and providing human support when it doesn't.Because for a patient struggling to connect, navigate an app, remember an OTP or make a digital payment, the smartphone should never become another obstacle between them and a doctor.
Article Summary: Digital health has opened up several ways for patients to manage their care remotely. People can consult doctors online, monitor blood sugar through connected devices, and access diet and educational resources without making frequent hospital visits. But for others, particularly older people, rural communities, low-income families and those with limited digital literacy, the shift can add another layer of difficulty.

Article Title: Punjab CM launches 'Mann Da Munafa' door-to-door campaign highlighting welfare initiatives

Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann on Sunday launched the AAP's door-to-door election campaign for the 2027 Punjab assembly polls, pitching his government's 'Mann Da Munafa' narrative, claiming that every family is receiving an annual benefit of Rs 1.82 lakh from its welfare initiatives like free electricity and healthcare.Mann said the AAP would go to every household with its record of work undertaken since 2022, while asserting that the campaign would remain positive and focus on what the government has delivered for Punjab.He said the AAP would seek people's support based on the work delivered on the ground and question the opposition over its record and the issue of combating drugs.During the outreach, Mann went door-to-door in Dhuri, met several families and interacted with elderly residents, women, youngsters and children.He listened to their views, discussed the work undertaken by the government over the past four-and-a-half years and explained how various schemes and initiatives were translating into direct benefits for ordinary households."Every family in Punjab is today benefiting by Rs 1.82 lakh annually from the initiatives rolled out by our government. This is not an abstract figure. It represents money a household no longer has to take out of its own pocket for electricity, healthcare, education and other essential services," he said."I want every family to sit down and calculate for itself how much it is saving every month. That is the real meaning of 'Mann Da Munafa'," Mann added.Claiming that his welfare initiatives reduced the financial burden of essential services on families, the chief minister said the government allowed them to use their hard-earned money for other household needs."Free electricity, healthcare, education, and Maavan Dheeyan Satkar Yojna are helping people save their hard-earned money. Lakhs of households across Punjab are receiving zero electricity bills, which means that money that earlier went towards electricity charges can now be spent on children, homes and farms," he said."The expansion of primary healthcare has also meant that a fever, a check-up or a basic diagnostic test does not have to force a family to borrow money or dip into its savings," Mann added.He said improvements in government schools have given parents greater confidence to educate their children without the burden of private fees."For decades, the people of Punjab paid taxes without receiving facilities in proportion to what they contributed. Our government is working to close that gap by directing resources towards households rather than privilege," the CM said."Mann Da Munafa is a simple question for every family: how much better off is your household today than it was before? Calculate what you save every month, and that answer will speak louder than any campaign speech," he said.Speaking about rural development, Mann said his government changed how resources were allocated to villages and made village-level development a central part of its approach.On the campaign strategy, he said AAP would keep its election campaign focused on its governance record rather than personal attacks or negativity."Our entire election campaign will remain positive. We will talk only about our work. We will place our record before the people and let them judge it, rather than build a campaign on abuse and negativity," he said."Our workers and candidates will carry the same message into every constituency: the savings delivered to families, the villages developed and public money spent on public welfare," he added.He said the door-to-door outreach provided the most direct opportunity for political representatives to account for their work before the people, adding that the campaign would be taken across Punjab, with party workers and candidates presenting the government's record directly before households.On the opposition, Mann said, "Congress is fighting among itself in Punjab, with its leaders more occupied with internal contests than with the concerns of the people, while the Shiromani Akali Dal has been wiped out and no longer commands a presence on the ground."On the issue of drugs, Mann questioned the BJP's position, claiming that drugs are being brought into Punjab from Gujarat."With what face is the BJP talking about drugs when it is bringing drugs into Punjab from Gujarat, he asked. PTI

Article Title: Delhi pollution crackdown: Hotspots to be mapped, pending road works get Oct 31 deadline
Article Text:
A thick layer of smog engulfs the India Gate and Kartavya Path as pollution level deteriorates, in New Delhi.

Hotspots to get source-specific action plans

October 31 target for pending road works

Construction, waste burning face tighter action

Illegal parking and encroachments targeted

Patparganj gets special focus

Future roads to minimise exposed soil

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Delhi government has stepped up its crackdown on air pollution, directing district administrations to map pollution hotspots, identify sources within a three-kilometre radius and assign agencies specific corrective measures and deadlines. The government has also set October 31 as the target for completing pending road and civil works, wherever feasible. It ordered tighter action against road dust, construction pollution, waste burning, illegal parking and traffic congestion.The directions were issued during district-level review meetings chaired by Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa for East, North-East, South-East and South Delhi. Officials were told to use AQI monitoring data to identify problem areas, assess the sources driving pollution and take immediate action at the ground level.District administrations will map pollution hotspots based on data from AQI monitoring stations. Each hotspot will then be assessed for sources such as road dust, traffic congestion, vehicular emissions, construction and demolition activity, unauthorised parking, open or uncovered areas and biomass or waste burning.Where applicable, pollution-generating activities within a three-kilometre radius of each hotspot will also be examined.Authorities will prepare source-wise action plans setting out the remedial measure, the agency responsible and the timeline for implementation.Locations recording high levels of PM10 and PM2.5 will receive focused attention, particularly areas with heavy traffic, heavy-vehicle parking, significant road dust and congestion. Such locations will be inspected for their pollution sources and immediate remedial action will be taken.The government has directed agencies to complete pending civil works on priority and by October 31, wherever feasible.These include pothole repairs, treatment and development of brown areas and other road and roadside works. Officials have also been told to maintain completed works properly to reduce road-dust generation.Where essential works cannot be completed because other projects are still underway, agencies will have to continue water sprinkling and other dust-suppression measures until the road surface is restored.The government has directed agencies to strictly enforce dust-control norms at construction and demolition sites. Violations will attract stringent action under applicable rules.The ban on biomass burning will also be enforced without exception. Preventive measures will be strengthened against the open burning of garbage, plastic and rubber waste, textile and fibre waste, industrial and organic residues, scrap and other combustible material.Officials were also directed to remove illegal encroachments from roads and public spaces where they contribute to congestion and obstruct traffic movement.The move is aimed at improving traffic flow and reducing pollution caused by idling vehicles and prolonged traffic movement.At Anand Vihar Bus Terminal, agencies have been directed to step up enforcement against unauthorised parking of buses and heavy vehicles. Cranes will be deployed wherever required to remove or tow such vehicles.Patparganj Industrial Area was identified for area-specific measures targeting road dust, traffic congestion and vehicular emissions.Agencies have been directed to maintain continuous water sprinkling and dust-control measures at vulnerable locations, particularly where road or allied works are underway.For future applicable works, departments have been directed to incorporate end-to-end carpeting or paving of roads and relevant roadside areas wherever technically feasible and in accordance with applicable specifications.The aim is to reduce exposed soil and unpaved surfaces that can contribute to road dust.The government has stressed closer coordination between departments and agencies, with responsibility for individual pollution-control measures clearly assigned.The meetings involved area MLAs, district magistrates, deputy commissioners of police, MCD deputy commissioners and senior officials from various departments.Officials from the Revenue Department, DPCC, PWD, MCD, Traffic Police, DSIIDC, I&FC, DJB, DMRC, NHAI and other agencies were involved in the coordinated effort.The minister also directed ground teams to maintain regular vigilance at vulnerable locations and take immediate action against violations. DPCC and enforcement agencies were asked to impose stringent penalties, including heavy challans wherever applicable.Officials were further told to ensure prompt resolution of citizen complaints, particularly those received through Helpline 311.
Article Summary: District administrations will map pollution hotspots based on data from AQI monitoring stations. Each hotspot will be assessed for sources such as road dust, traffic congestion, vehicular emissions, construction and demolition activity, unauthorised parking, open or uncovered areas and biomass or waste burning.

NEW DELHI: Indian Air Chief Marshal Amar Preet Singh and Japan Air Self-Defence Force Chief of Staff General Takehiro Morita took sorties on Tejas fighter aircraft on Sunday.This comes amid the ongoing Indo-Japan bilateral air exercise 'Veer Guardian-2026' at Air Force Station Jodhpur in Rajasthan.The IAF is participating with a mix of frontline combat aircraft, including the indigenous Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Tejas, Su-30MKI and Rafale fighter jets, while the JASDF has deployed its F-2A fighter aircraft.The exercise, which began on September 9 and will continue till September 22, involves advanced operational missions, mission planning and professional exchanges between personnel of the two air forces.The participation of Japanese fighter aircraft in the exercise marks the first time JASDF combat aircraft have operated from Indian soil.Earlier, on September 10, defence minister Rajnath Singh described Japan sending its fighter aircraft to participate in Exercise Veer Guardian as a "significant milestone" for the India-Japan defence partnership.In a post on X, he said the maiden visit of Japan Air Self-Defence Force fighter aircraft to India reflected growing trust and a shared commitment to peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific.He also recalled his "highly productive discussions" with his Japanese counterpart in New Delhi last month, saying exchanges such as Exercise Veer Guardian would further strengthen cooperation between the two countries.The Indian Air Force had welcomed the Japanese F-2 fighter jets to Jodhpur on September 8 ahead of the exercise. NEW DELHI: Congress on Sunday took a swipe at Union home minister Amit Shah over the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, alleging that it was a "Shah Instigated Removal" of voters.Congress general secretary in-charge of communications Jairam Ramesh said the Election Commission began Phase 1 of the SIR process in Bihar in June 2025, followed by Phase 2 in November 2025 across nine states and three Union Territories.According to Jairam Ramesh, 7.8 crore names were deleted during the first two phases, amounting to 13% of the pre-SIR electoral roll.Jairam said Phase 3 began in 16 states and three Union Territories in mid-2026. Citing data from 12 states and two UTs, he claimed that 6.18 crore names had been deleted from a total of 36.06 crore voters."The deletion rate works out to over 17% 2. An additional 5.43 crore voters have been issued notices demanding additional documentation to have their names retained on the electoral roll. The risk of deletion rate works to another 15%. This is an unusually high proportion that reflects structural flaws in the entire SIR process," Jairam said.He questioned how such a large number of voters could still be required to undergo verification after the deletion of millions of names."Thus, a staggering 32% (or about one in three) of voters have had their names deleted or face risk of deletion," Jairam added.He cited Delhi, Chandigarh, Jharkhand, Uttarakhand, Meghalaya, Maharashtra, Telangana, Karnataka, Haryana, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Punjab as states and UTs where he claimed a significant proportion of voters had either been deleted or faced the risk of deletion.The Congress leader also alleged that large-scale deletions were disproportionately affecting voters from economically and socially disadvantaged sections. He further claimed that, in most major states, more women than men had been removed from electoral rolls during the SIR process.Jairam said the exercise had shifted the burden of verification from the state to citizens, who were being asked to produce documents that they may never have been issued. "A test that the overwhelming majority of citizens cannot pass is just a 'machine for exclusion'," he said."SIR is actually a massive Shah Instigated Removal of voters. It is an assault on our Constitution," he added.Tagging his statement on X, he wrote, "SIR is actually a Shah Instigated Removal of voters on a massive scale. Here is a statement on this brazen assault on our Constitution itself."Jairam also said voter lists facing deletion risks had been made publicly available in Karnataka, Telangana and Jharkhand, allowing voters to check their names. He claimed Delhi made its list public only on September 19, 2026, following public pressure, while other BJP-ruled states and Punjab had not done so.The Election Commission has maintained that the SIR, being conducted after 22 years, is aimed at cleaning electoral rolls by removing ineligible and duplicate entries while ensuring that all eligible citizens are included in the rolls.Opposition parties have alleged that the exercise could target voters who do not support the BJP and its allies. The allegations have been rejected by the Election Commission, which has defended the revision as an exercise to ensure accurate and legally eligible electoral rolls.
Article Summary: Congress general secretary in-charge of communications Jairam Ramesh said the Election Commission began Phase 1 of the SIR process in Bihar in June 2025. He claimed that 6.18 crore names had been deleted from a total of 36.06 crore voters. The Election Commission has defended the revision as an exercise to ensure accurate and legally eligible electoral rolls.

Article Title: Morning-after pills may get 4 boxed warnings
Article Text:
The proposed warnings will also caution that frequent use may lead to side effects

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Morning-after pills containing levonorgestrel may soon carry four prominent boxed warnings. Govt has proposed that the pills should be labelled clearly as meant only for emergency use, not as regular contraception, not as abortion pills and not as protection against HIV or other sexually transmitted infections.The proposed warnings will also caution that frequent use may lead to side effects and advise users seeking regular contraception to visit a health facility or a registered medical practitioner.Dr Megha Tiwari, Consultant, Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Kailash Hospital & Neuro Institute, said emergency contraceptive pills are an important and safe option when used appropriately, but concerns arise when they start being treated as routine contraception. "We do see women taking it repeatedly after unprotected intercourse, sometimes without understanding that it can disturb the menstrual cycle and cause temporary bleeding irregularities, nausea or anxiety around a delayed period," she said."The bigger issue is misinformation. Some women believe the pill can terminate an existing pregnancy, while others assume it offers protection against HIV or other sexually transmitted infections, which it does not," Tiwari said.She added that the proposed warnings were less about creating fear around emergency contraception and more about ensuring women understood its correct role as a backup method after contraceptive failure, rather than a replacement for regular contraception or condoms.The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has proposed the changes through a draft amendment to Drugs Rules, 1945, covering levonorgestrel tablets of 0.75 mg and 1.5 mg. The warnings would have to appear prominently both on the packaging and the package insert.The proposal also seeks to add levonorgestrel tablets 0.75 mg and 1.5 mg as a specific entry under Schedule K of Drugs Rules, along with conditions relating to their exemption from sale-licence requirements.However, the warnings are not yet mandatory. The notification is a draft, with 30 days invited for objections and suggestions.
Article Summary: The proposed warnings will also caution that frequent use may lead to side effects. The warnings would have to appear prominently both on the packaging and the package insert. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has proposed the changes through a draft amendment to Drugs Rules, 1945.

NEW DELHI: The southwest (summer) monsoon, which has so far reported a nationwide deficit of 15% in cumulative (June 1-Sept 19) rainfall, started withdrawing from west Rajasthan Saturday, as against the normal date of Sept 17, IMD has said.The line of withdrawal Saturday passed through Ramgarh, Mohangarh, Phalodi and Khajuwala. "Conditions are also favourable for further withdrawal from some more parts of Rajasthan and some parts of Punjab and Saurashtra and Kachchh over the next three-four days," said the Met department.The monsoon normally starts withdrawing from Sept 17 and the process ends on Oct 15 - a few days ahead of the onset of the winter monsoon in peninsular India.As many as 14 states, including Bihar, Punjab, Haryana and all five peninsular states, have reported a rain deficit of more than 20% so far. The current situation shows that the monsoon season is likely to end on Sept 30 with an overall deficit of more than 10% in the country as a whole - a level of rain deficiency which is considered a drought - even as the low pressure area and subsequent depression over east central Bay of Bengal may cause good rain in east India and coastal Odisha next week.Although the sowing of kharif (summer-sown) crops has progressed well despite the El Nino-linked rain deficit, it does not mean the crop sector is out of danger as regional variations and the skewed timing of rainfall may impact overall yield and sowing during next crop (rabi) season. El Nino, a climatic phenomenon involving the warming of ocean surface temperatures in central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is invariably associated with a harsh summer and weak monsoon in India.Acreage data Friday shows that though the overall sown area for all kharif crops has declined this year by just a little over 1%, water-intensive paddy - the most important seasonal crop that accounts for the most acreage - reported a decline of nearly 4% compared to the corresponding period last year.

NEW DELHI: PM Narendra Modi Saturday questioned the narrative in which the responsibility for carbon emissions is pinned on developing countries while Western countries are absolved of their role as historical polluters, even as he reaffirmed the country’s commitment to climate action and stressed that it has the best record among G20 countries. “In developed countries, per capita carbon emissions are six times higher than India’s... India presents this fact strongly on global platforms... We are establishing new benchmarks for environmental protection by taking the world along,” he said. His remarks at an international conference on ‘The Future of Environment and Climate Dynamics’, organised by NGT, come as the world gears up for the global climate conference scheduled for Nov in Turkiye.He said India is providing solutions to modern climate challenges even as its per capita carbon emissions are less than half of the global average.The PM’s remarks are being seen as a pushback against the West’s attempt, despite its historical responsibility for alarming emission levels, to suggest that India needs to accept stiff emission-reduction targets. Article Title: He moved to Canada and rented his Punjab house for Rs 20,000 a month, then sought eviction to use it during India visits; Punjab & Haryana HC rules against landlord, allows tenant to stay
Article Text:
Court ruled in favour of the tenant and rejected the landlord’s plea seeking her eviction. (Image for representative purpose only)

What the case is about

Why did the landlord lose the tenant eviction case?

What are the landlord’s options?

He moved to Canada and rented his Punjab house for Rs 20,000 a month, then sought eviction to use it during India visits; Punjab & Haryana HC rules against landlord, allows tenant to stayA man owned a residential property in Jagraon, Punjab, which he rented out after moving to Canada. A lady became the tenant and paid Rs 20,000 a month in rent. The arrangement continued without any reported issue until the man decided that he wanted the property back.He sought to regain possession because he wanted to use the house for himself during his visits to India. He therefore asked the woman to vacate the property. She declined, following which the owner approached the court and initiated eviction proceedings against his tenant.After the case went through a prolonged legal battle, the Punjab and Haryana High Court ruled in favour of the tenant and rejected the landlord’s plea seeking her eviction.Here is a closer look at the dispute and the reasons given by the high court for deciding the case in favour of the tenant.The man had purchased the property in 2012 and initially lived there himself. After moving to Canada in 2020, he rented the house to the woman.A year later, in 2021, he asked her to leave the property.According to the landlord, he needed the house for his own use because he frequently faced difficulty finding suitable accommodation whenever he travelled to India. The tenant, however, refused to vacate the premises.The man subsequently filed an eviction petition against her on April 29, 2021, invoking Section 13 B of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949. He claimed the benefit of the provision on the ground that he was a Non-Resident Indian permanently settled in Canada.The rent controller accepted the landlord’s plea and, on August 12, 2021, directed the woman to vacate the property, according to an ET report.Facing the prospect of losing the home, the tenant challenged the eviction order before the Punjab and Haryana High Court. The high court ruled in her favour on September 7, 2026, rejecting the eviction claim and allowing her to remain in the property.Abhiraj Gandhi, Partner at Khaitan & Co, told ET that the landlord’s eviction plea failed because he sought to remove the tenant by relying on a legal provision meant for NRI landlords that had already been repealed.The central issue was that the man filed the eviction petition on April 29, 2021 under Section 13-B of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949. However, the relevant provision under that law had been repealed on November 30, 2013. The tenancy in this case began only on January 17, 2020, more than six years after the repeal had taken effect.After this issue came to light, the landlord attempted to change the legal basis of his case. He sought to rely instead on the Punjab Rent Act, 1995, which replaced the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act with effect from November 30, 2013. The court, however, did not accept this change either.Gandhi explained that the landlord could not invoke the corresponding special remedy available to NRI landlords under Section 24(3) of the Punjab Rent Act, 1995. That provision applies when the premises were let out on or before the commencement of the 1995 Act and the NRI owner subsequently returns to India for permanent residence. Since the tenancy in this case began in 2020, it did not fall within the specific scope of Section 24(3).Section 75 of the Punjab Rent Act, 1995 does preserve rights and proceedings that had already arisen or were in existence under the repealed law.However, Gandhi said this provision cannot be used to create a new right under legislation after that legislation has been repealed. In this case, there was neither an existing tenancy nor a pending eviction proceeding relating to the property on November 30, 2013. Therefore, no right under Section 13-B had accrued to him that could subsequently be preserved.The landlord also put forward an alternative argument that the property was exempt from the Punjab Rent Act, 1995. Gandhi explained that the exemption under Section 3(1)(c) is determined by the date on which construction was completed, rather than the date on which the land was purchased.The landlord had relied on his purchase of the plot in 2012. However, he failed to establish the legally relevant completion date through the completion intimation or property-tax assessment required under the Act. The Rent Controller had also not made a specific finding on this issue.Gandhi further pointed out that even if the property were eventually held to fall outside the scope of the 1995 Act, this would not bring back Section 13-B of the repealed 1949 legislation. In that situation, the landlord would have to pursue the remedies available under the general law governing exempt premises.The High Court also identified a procedural problem in the proceedings. The Rent Controller had effectively reconsidered an earlier order even though no statutory power of review had been conferred on the authority.In any event, the eviction order could not stand because the original petition itself was not maintainable under the legal provision on whichThe High Court has overturned the eviction order because the petition was not maintainable, without examining whether the landlord actually needed the property for his own use.The court has, however, left the door open for him to pursue any other remedy available to him under the applicable law.Gandhi told ET that the landlord's first priority in any new proceedings would be to determine which legal framework applies to the property.If he seeks to claim the 15-year exemption under Section 3(1)(c) of the 1995 Act, he will have to establish the date on which construction was completed in the manner specified under the law. This would primarily require the completion intimation submitted to the relevant authority or the first property-tax assessment, whichever occurred earlier. The 15-year exemption is calculated from that date and not from the date when the plot was purchased.If the property is established to fall within the exemption, Gandhi said the landlord could seek eviction under the general law applicable to exempt premises, subject to the terms of the tenancy documents and other applicable legal requirements.If the property does not qualify for the exemption, the landlord would instead have to proceed under the Punjab Rent Act, 1995. In that situation, he would need to independently establish one of the ordinary statutory grounds for eviction provided under the Act.
Article Summary: Man owned a residential property in Jagraon, Punjab, which he rented out after moving to Canada. A lady became the tenant and paid Rs 20,000 a month in rent. The arrangement continued without any reported issue until the man decided that he wanted the property back. He sought to regain possession because he wanted to use the house for himself during his visits to India. Punjab & Haryana HC rules against landlord, allows tenant to stay.

Article Title: India-Japan air exercise Veer Guardian signals growing strategic alignment in the Indo-Pacific
Article Text:
JASDF Chief of Staff Masahiro Morita and IAF Chief of Air Staff AP Singh at Jodhpur Air Force Base during Ex Veer Guardian. (Image credit: IAF)

The successful conclusion of Exercise Veer Guardian 2026 has once again put the spotlight on just how far the India-Japan defence relationship has come, evolving from routine military exchanges into a genuinely comprehensive strategic partnership spanning operational cooperation, defence technology, maritime security and emerging military capabilities.This latest edition carried added weight because Japanese fighter aircraft operated from Indian soil for the very first time, a genuine milestone in the growing military engagement between the Indian Air Force and the Japan Air Self-Defense Force. Beyond the air combat drills, the exercise served as a visible demonstration of the trust, interoperability and strategic convergence steadily building between two of the Indo-Pacific's most important powers, both of whom share overlapping concerns about regional security.JASDF Chief General Takehiro Morita flew a sortie in a twin-seat variant of India's indigenous Tejas Light Combat Aircraft, calling it a symbol of India's technological innovation, a clear signal of Japan's appreciation for the country's growing aerospace capabilities. IAF Chief Air Chief Marshal AP Singh, for his part, led a Tejas formation flight during the exercise, underscoring both his own confidence in the indigenous platform and just how operationally mature the aircraft has become.For New Delhi and Tokyo, Veer Guardian represents far more than an air force engagement, it's one visible piece of a defence relationship that has expanded considerably over the past decade. Air Chief Marshal Singh's description of Japan as an "Apatsu Mitram," a friend in times of crisis, captured the level of strategic trust now underpinning bilateral ties. Both nations are Quad members, sharing a commitment to a free, open and rules-based Indo-Pacific, an outlook that has steadily translated into deeper cooperation across all three services. Apart from Veer Guardian, the armies of the two nations conduct Exercise Dharma Guardian, while the navies regularly engage through JAIMEX and the multilateral MILAN exercise.This growing military relationship rests on a series of agreements signed, covering defence cooperation and exchanges, equipment and technology transfers, protection of classified military information, and a Reciprocal Provision of Supplies and Services agreement, all of which have collectively enabled smoother logistics support and interoperability.Defence technology cooperation has also gained real momentum, with the two countries signing their first joint defence equipment project in 2024 an agreement to co-develop the UNICORN mast system for the Indian Navy's warships. The mast integrates radar and communication antennas into a single structure that reduces a warship's radar signature while improving efficiency, thus making the vessel a more effective combatant.Japan's transport aircraft and maritime patrol platforms an be another area of common interest for India. This opens up genuine opportunities for co-development and co-production under the Make in India framework, potentially letting Japanese firms tap into India's manufacturing ecosystem for both domestic and export markets.The recent visit of Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi added further weight to this trajectory. In talks with Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, the two sides signed a Memorandum of Arrangement on maritime security cooperation, focused on maritime domain awareness, information sharing, and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief. Discussions also touched on mine countermeasures, shipbuilding, reciprocal ship repair facilities and joint defence research.The dialogue has even extended into next-generation technologies, with India examining pathways for future combat aviation capabilities, and reports suggesting discussions around potential Indian participation in Japan's Global Combat Air Programme, its sixth-generation fighter initiative. This programme is still at the exploratory stage and India is also in talks with France over the Future Combat Air System platform.Exercise Veer Guardian stands as a clear marker of a partnership that is increasingly operational, technology-driven and strategically significant. As both India and Japan deepen military cooperation amid a shifting Indo-Pacific security landscape.
Article Summary: The successful conclusion of Exercise Veer Guardian 2026 put the spotlight on just how far the India-Japan defence relationship has come. The exercise served as a visible demonstration of the trust, interoperability and strategic convergence steadily building between two of the Indo-Pacific's most important powers.

Article Title: World's last known wild Chilean tree daisy gets a lifeline as conservationists use ropes to support its only survivor and two seedlings arrive at a Scottish garden
Article Text:
Image: Wikimedia

World's rarest wild Chilean tree daisy clings to life

Scientists collect 29 seeds from the last known wild tree

Image: BBC

Two seedlings arrive at Logan Botanic Garden in Scotland

International conservationists work against extinction

Why scientists are growing the seedlings outside Chile

Conservation efforts offer hope for the species

A rare tree daisy from Chile's Robinson Crusoe Island is receiving a new lifeline after two seedlings arrived at Logan Botanic Garden in south-west Scotland. Dendroseris neriifolia has been reduced to one known wild tree, which grows on a steep cliff and is supported by ropes to prevent it from falling. Conservationists in Chile and the UK are working to preserve the species through seed collection and cultivation. In May 2026, 29 seeds were collected from the surviving tree and sent to Kew's Millennium Seed Bank. Eight seedlings germinated, and two have since been transferred to Logan, where specialists hope to learn more about their growth and help secure the future of the critically endangered plant.The remaining wild Dendroseris neriifolia tree grows on a steep volcanic outcrop on Robinson Crusoe Island. Its precarious position has made physical support essential, with ropes helping prevent the tree from falling. The species has experienced a sharp decline over several decades. By 1980, only eight wild trees remained. Reintroduction projects were attempted in the early 2000s, but the breakdown of protective measures in 2017 allowed invasive plants and grazing animals to threaten the site again.The Chilean tree daisy has been affected by widespread forest clearance, intensive grazing by introduced mammals, invasive vegetation and repeated fires.These pressures have damaged the natural habitat on which the species depends. Robinson Crusoe Island is part of the Juan Fernández Archipelago, a group of islands recognised for its distinctive native flora. The restricted distribution of Dendroseris neriifolia makes the loss of its remaining wild population particularly significant.In May 2026, conservationists collected 29 seeds from the surviving tree and sent them to the Millennium Seed Bank at Kew Wakehurst in England. Kew's analysis found that 25 seeds were potentially viable. Eight seedlings subsequently germinated. The work provides an opportunity to preserve plant material from the wild survivor and investigate cultivation methods for the species. The seed collection is part of a broader conservation effort that includes previous collections and restoration projects intended to support the recovery of the tree daisy on its native island. Though only a single wild tree remains, these eight young seedlings offer a hopeful first step toward securing the future of the tree daisy.Two of the germinated seedlings have now been transferred to Logan Botanic Garden in Dumfries and Galloway. The remaining germinated plants will stay at Kew and Logan is known for its mild climate, which allows it to cultivate plants from warmer regions. Its experience with species from the Juan Fernández Islands makes it a suitable location for growing the young tree daisies. Richard Baines, curator at Logan, said the arrival of the seedlings was a significant moment for everyone involved. He explained that the garden would provide a safe place for the plants while specialists learn more about their development and adaptation to different environments.The project involves conservationists and scientists from Chile and the UK. Jardín Botánico VerdeNativo, Chile's National Forest Corporation and the Juan Fernández National Park are among the organisations involved in the conservation effort. Diego Penneckamp, a scientist at Jardín Botánico VerdeNativo, described the work as a race against time. He said the international collaboration could help prevent the extinction of a species with a unique evolutionary history. Felipe Saez, a plant biotechnology engineer and administrator of Parque Nacional Archipiélago Juan Fernández, also highlighted the significance of the seed transfer for protecting the archipelago's native plant life.The seedlings at Logan and Kew provide a form of ex-situ conservation, which involves protecting species outside their natural habitats. This approach can help safeguard plants when wild populations face severe threats.Growing the seedlings to maturity could allow researchers to study their development and potentially produce additional seeds. However, the long-term success of the programme will depend on the plants' ability to survive, reproduce and contribute to future conservation work.The wider Dendroseris genus is endemic to the Juan Fernández Islands. Kew has also identified conservation concerns affecting other species within the genus, underscoring the importance of protecting the archipelago's unique biodiversity.The arrival of two seedlings at Logan Botanic Garden marks a new stage in the effort to preserve Dendroseris neriifolia. The wild tree remains on Robinson Crusoe Island, where ropes are helping protect it from falling, while its offspring are being cultivated in the UK.The project combines field conservation in Chile with seed banking and horticultural expertise in Britain. By maintaining plants outside the wild, conservationists hope to develop a stronger foundation for protecting the species and supporting its future recovery.
Article Summary: Dendroseris neriifolia has been reduced to one known wild tree on Robinson Crusoe Island. Conservationists in Chile and the UK are working to preserve the species through seed collection and cultivation. In May 2026, 29 seeds were collected from the surviving tree and sent to Kew's Millennium Seed Bank. Eight seedlings germinated, and two have since been transferred to Logan Botanic Garden in south-west Scotland.
