Article Title: Canadian billionaire Kevin O' Leary: Follow this rule, and you will be a millionaire when you retire
Article Text:
How Kevin O’Leary’s 15% savings rule works

Why saving 15% can be difficult for average workers

What a $68,000 salary looks like after basic expenses

How Warren Buffett’s advice compares

Kevin O’Leary has suggested a simple rule for Americans looking to build a seven-figure retirement portfolio. The Shark Tank US judge has recommended saving and investing 15% of every paycheque and letting the money compound over time. For someone earning $68,000 a year, the investor says consistently following that approach could result in a millionaire-sized retirement portfolio by age 65. The Canadian investor and entrepreneur recently shared the advice in an Instagram post, telling people to put money into the market rather than spend it on things they do not need. His calculation assumes decades of consistent investing and relies on long-term stock market growth.“What piece of advice do I give my kids over and over and over again about money? Don't spend it. Save it, invest it, let it compound. That's the gift the market gives you. Take 15% of all your paycheques, all your side hustle, any cash Granny gives you, put it in the market, and just let it compound. If you make $68,000 a year, the average salary, and you do this your entire life, just 15% of your paycheque- you'll end up a millionaire by retirement in '65.Best piece of advice I can give anybody. Don't buy stuff you don't need; invest it instead. Cheers,” O’Leary said in the post.By his example of an income of $68,000, that would mean a 15 per cent contribution of roughly $10,200 a year, or $850 a month. If you invested that amount consistently for 40 years, from age 25 to 65, your portfolio could grow substantially with compound returns.The strategy is straightforward on paper, but putting aside 15% of income can be difficult for households already dealing with rent, food, student loans and other living costs.The calculation depends heavily on investment returns and how long the money stays invested. Assuming an average annual return of about 10%, broadly in line with the S&P 500's historical long-term average, investing $850 every month for 40 years would produce approximately $5.3 million.At a lower assumed average return of 7 per cent, that same monthly contribution would have accumulated to about $2.2 million over four decades. In either case, the investor would have more than $1 million at retirement. Remember that actual investment returns can vary from year to year and are not guaranteed.So O’Leary’s estimate is an illustration of long-term compounding rather than a guaranteed outcome. It also assumes the worker can contribute uninterrupted over a 40-year career.The challenge is less about the arithmetic than whether an average household can consistently set aside that much money. Workers earning between $50,000 and $79,999 are among those most likely to report falling behind on retirement savings, with 55% saying they feel behind.According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the personal savings rate was 4.4% of disposable income in mid-2025, a Fortune report noted. For a $68,000 earner, that would be about $3,000 a year, a far cry from the $10,200 annual investment suggested by O’Leary’s 15% rule.Vanguard data also show that the median total contribution rate among 401(k) participants, including employee and employer contributions, is about 11.5%. That figure applies mainly to workers with access to a 401(k), so it does not represent the entire workforce.An American household making $68,000 before taxes will take home about $52,000 to $54,000 after federal and state taxes. This will leave about $3,600 a month for other expenses.Average US rent is about $1,740 a month, according to RentCafe. That would leave around $1,860 before other household costs. Groceries can add as much as $400 a month for a single person based on Bureau of Labour Statistics data, reducing the amount further.The remaining amount could drop to around $726 with student loan payments averaging about $434 a month and utilities at about $300. That would mean that saving $850 a month would be more than what you would have left after all of the expenses above.Even if the calculation is based on 15% of take-home income rather than gross pay, the target is still substantial. Nearly $52,000 in annual take-home income is about $650 a month at 15 per cent, which might still leave only about $150 in discretionary income under the expense assumptions.O’Leary agrees with Buffett’s long-term, low-cost approach to investing. Buffett has said that on the whole, average investors are better off with low-cost S&P 500 index funds than paying high fees to professional managers.“Put 10% of the cash in short-term government bonds and 90% in a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund. (I suggest Vanguard’s),” Buffett wrote in a 2013 shareholders’ letter. “I believe the trust’s long-term results from this policy.”
Article Summary: Shark Tank US judge recommends saving and investing 15% of every paycheque and letting the money compound over time. For someone earning $68,000 a year, the investor says consistently following that approach could result in a millionaire-sized retirement portfolio by age 65.

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang rejects Dario Amodei and Sam Altman’s 'AI will kill us all warnings': ‘Don't let this doomsday narrative cause somebody to…’
Article Text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

Jensen Huang says ‘no’ to 2030 extinction threat

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has outrightly rejected the apocalyptic claims that artificial intelligence (AI) will cause the extinction of humanity in the coming years, dismissing such warnings as baseless and exaggerated scare tactics. Speaking with CBS News, Huang challenged these ‘doomsday predictions’ voiced by prominent tech leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, cautioning the public and lawmakers not to be misled by panic.“Don't let this doomsday narrative cause somebody to relieve them of the laws that currently exist," Huang stated in an interview, adding, “Read between the lines. They're actually not asking for more laws. They're asking to be relieved of the laws we do have. And I think that that's a problem. We have plenty of laws, so let's apply those first.”Huang’s comments follow a heated public dispute triggered earlier this month by Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic. Coxon posted on social media that developers of frontier AI models believe the technology could wipe out humanity before the decade concludes.This ignited widespread controversy and prompted Amodei, Altman and Elon Musk to urge a deliberate slow down in model development.Huang flatly rejected those forecasts, arguing they have no grounding in scientific reality.“2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that's going to be the end of the world. Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible,” Huang added.As the biggest producer of specialised chips powering AI models developed by OpenAI and competing labs, Nvidia holds an immense financial stake in the conversation. Soaring demand for its graphics processors has driven the company's valuation to $5.3 trillion, solidifying its rank as the world's most valuable enterprise.When asked why the public should accept his safety assurances given Nvidia’s obvious financial motives, Huang maintained that corporate health depends entirely on dependable technology.“Our company's success is directly connected to the safe deployment of products and services. If we don't continue to do that, our value would be diminished,” he noted.Huang also said that current American frameworks dealing with unauthorised computer access, damage liabilities and product safety are more than adequate.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang says ‘no’ to 2030 extinction threat. ‘There is 0% chance that's going to be the end of the world. Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible,’ he said. Huang’s comments follow a heated public dispute triggered by Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic.

Article Title: Anthropic, CEO of which called for slowing AI development, may release new model ahead of IPO
Article Text:
OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra shakes up enterprise spending

Anthropic is reportedly weighing the release of a new artificial intelligence (AI) model to counter the rising momentum of rival OpenAI’s newly deployed GPT-6 Astra, a report has said, citing three people familiar with internal discussions. The potential rollout comes ahead of an anticipated initial public offering (IPO) and arrives two weeks after Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei released a 3,800-word essay urging the global AI ecosystem to curb the speed of frontier model releases out of concern for systemic safety risks.As per a report by news agency Reuters, the internal push to deploy a countermeasure highlights the fierce commercial rivalry between the two frontier developers. Amodei warned of dark scenarios involving swarms of autonomous AI agents hacking websites without human oversight. This stance received public backing from OpenAI chief Sam Altman and SpaceX head Elon Musk.Now, Anthropic finds itself balancing those cautionary declarations against intense market pressure, with internal teams evaluating the safety benchmarks of its next system while deliberating whether to greenlight a launch, the report noted.OpenAI rolled out GPT-6 Astra on September 3, highlighting significant leaps in autonomous computer use, coding, professional workplace tools and cybersecurity. The launch has reportedly seen rapid adoption across corporate clients. Data tracked by corporate expense platform Ramp shows GPT-6 Astra capturing approximately 13% of monitored enterprise AI expenditures, compared to roughly 8% for Anthropic’s Claude Fable.Despite OpenAI's recent gains, several current backers and funds preparing to invest in both upcoming IPOs argue that Astra does not present an existential threat to Anthropic. Analysts point to the considerable time it takes for corporate clients to rip out and replace entrenched software vendors.Furthermore, Anthropic’s annualised revenue run rate climbed past $65 billion by late July, surging from approximately $9 billion at the close of 2025. In comparison, OpenAI's annualised revenue run rate crossed $40 billion in July.Beyond its direct duel with OpenAI, Anthropic faces broader structural challenges across the industry. For example, the rapid rise of open-source and open-weight alternatives from China gives businesses cheaper pathways to build internal infrastructure without paying premium token fees to proprietary providers.Major customers are also looking inward. Meta Platforms, historically one of Anthropic’s top enterprise accounts, is actively looking to scale back its reliance on Claude systems as it expands its own internal computing models.
Article Summary: Anthropic is reportedly weighing the release of a new artificial intelligence (AI) model to counter the rising momentum of rival OpenAI’s newly deployed GPT-6 Astra. The potential rollout comes ahead of an anticipated initial public offering (IPO) of Anthropic.

Article Title: Days after Michael Dell briefly became world’s second richest man, he is selling 4,100-sq-ft Boston penthouse that he purchased 10 years ago for $10.9 million
Article Text:
Michael Dell’s almost untouched luxury home

Could buyers land a bargain

Not Michael Dell's first headline-making property deal

Just days after Michael Dell briefly climbed to the position of the world’s second-richest man, the Dell Technologies founder is making headlines again — this time in real estate. Dell has put his 4,100-square-foot Boston penthouse on the market, a property he purchased a decade ago for $10.9 million. Located in Boston’s Millennium Tower, the penthouse offers sweeping city views, luxury finishes, and access to exclusive amenities. The residence reflects Dell’s penchant for high-value real estate investments, complementing his portfolio that includes properties in Texas and Hawaii. The listing comes amid Dell’s extraordinary financial year, with his net worth surging by more than $80 billion thanks to booming demand for AI infrastructure.Dell bought the Millennium Tower penthouse in 2016 through an LLC. Nearly a decade later, the roughly 4,100-square-foot, three-bedroom unit is heading to a sealed-bid auction with a reserve price $4.4 million below what he originally paid — a potential 41% discount from its last sale price.Bidding is open now and closes on October 29, though the property remains subject to a prior sale.Perched on the 59th floor of Millennium Tower, the penthouse comes with sweeping views and, according to the listing agent, has barely been lived in since Dell bought it. Notably, the home's oven has apparently never even been turned on.The sale comes at an interesting moment for Dell. His fortune took a $15.1 billion hit this past week as Dell Technologies shares fell amid a broader AI-stock selloff, knocking him down to No. 4 on Forbes' Real-Time Billionaires List. Just days earlier, he had briefly climbed to No. 2 on that same list for the first time. Despite the sharp drop, there's little to suggest the sale is driven by financial necessity — Dell remains one of the wealthiest people in the world.The auction is being handled by Paramount Realty USA in collaboration with SERHANT. Massachusetts. Paramount founder and CEO Misha Haghani acknowledged there's a real possibility a buyer could land a good deal, though he was careful to note that what counts as a "good deal" is ultimately subjective and will come down to how the market responds. Haghani declined to comment on why Dell is selling.This isn't Dell's first eye-catching real estate move. The Dell Technologies founder and CEO previously paid $100.47 million for a penthouse at Manhattan's One57 in 2014, a deal that set records at the time. His willingness to buy — and now sell — trophy properties at steep prices underscores a pattern of high-profile real estate bets that mirror the volatility of his tech fortune, which has swung dramatically in recent weeks alongside the broader AI-driven market turbulence hitting Dell Technologies stock.
Article Summary: Dell Technologies founder and CEO has put his 4,100-square-foot Boston penthouse on the market, a property he purchased a decade ago for $10.9 million. The penthouse offers sweeping city views, luxury finishes, and access to exclusive amenities. The residence reflects Dell’s penchant for high-value real estate investments, complementing his portfolio that includes properties in Texas and Hawaii.

Article Title: Oracle layoffs reach Abilene, the 'flagship' Stargate data center that Oracle keeps showing as proof the OpenAI deal is fine: Employee says he found out he was fired when...
Article Text:
Oracle employees lost Slack and VPN before the layoff email reached them

Abilene shows what Oracle's AI buildout costs on both sides of the ledger

Oracle's layoffs on September 14 reached Abilene, Texas, the site the company has spent months holding up as evidence that its OpenAI partnership is on track. One employee there, an IC2 in OCI who says he joined on February 2, described the morning on r/employeesOfOracle: the termination email arrived at 5am Central, he did not see it, and he only realised what had happened when his badge failed at the gate. His Slack was already locked. His last performance review had been "meets expectations". Another poster in the same thread said Customer Hardware Support was cut at Abilene, Phoenix and Ashburn.Abilene is not an incidental site. It is the flagship Stargate campus, the one Oracle cites when it talks about 200MW of operational capacity and an eight-building build running on schedule. It is also the site OpenAI has decided not to expand, preferring clusters with newer Nvidia chips, and the one lenders declined to finance with Oracle as tenant. Oracle does not own it. It leases the facility from Crusoe on a 15-year deal worth more than a billion dollars a year. Oracle has not commented on the cuts.The sequence was the same everywhere. Federated logins stopped working around 4am Eastern, Slack sessions dropped out between 5am and 5.30am, and the email from "Oracle Leadership" landed at 6am. Several people on the subreddit said they were locked out before they could read it.One OCI employee wrote that his login let him in for a second, then booted him out. Another found out from a text sent by a coworker while he was walking home from a run.The posts ran through the morning across OCI security, CI/CD, enterprise engineering, observability, executive escalations, Fusion, NetSuite sales, Customer Success Services, Oracle Health, EPM, HR Technology and data centre compliance. Employees tracked the Slack member count as it fell, putting the US drop at roughly 3,200 against Friday.Oracle severance works out to 4 weeks plus a week for every year servedOracle is offering four weeks of base salary plus one additional week per year of service. The March version of the plan capped the total at 26 weeks. The latest documents do not state a cap.That formula explains the numbers circulating on Reddit. A data centre technician with eight months reported four weeks. Someone with four years in the database org got seven and called it a kick in the nuts. An IC5 with 7.5 years got ten. By comparison, Salesforce's standard policy runs up to 30 weeks and Microsoft offered up to 39 weeks this summer.The money behind Abilene is what makes the cuts there awkward. Oracle reported $28.5 billion in first-quarter capital expenditure, against $8.5 billion a year earlier, and kept its fiscal 2027 forecast at $90 billion to $95 billion. It raised its restructuring plan by about $700 million on Friday, to roughly $2.8 billion, and tied part of that to AI adoption across some functions.Headcount had already fallen by 21,000 in the year to May 31, leaving about 141,000 staff before September 14. One employee on the subreddit, writing from Abilene, put it more plainly than any filing: he had previously worked at IBM and Microsoft, so he would be fine, he just had to get out of town first.
Article Summary: Abilene is the flagship Stargate campus, the one Oracle cites when it talks about 200MW of operational capacity and an eight-building build running on schedule. It is also the site OpenAI has decided not to expand, preferring clusters with newer Nvidia chips, and the one lenders declined to finance with Oracle as tenant.

Article Title: Apple Pay may launch in India next month: Report
Article Text:
Apple Pay may launch in India next month: Report

Will Apple Pay support UPI in India

Apple Pay has been in talks with Indian banks

Apple Pay could finally launch in India as early as October, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. In the latest edition of his Power On newsletter, Gurman said Apple is preparing to launch Apple Pay in India “finally” next month. The service is expected to support card payments, while there are also reports that Apple could bring UPI support to the platform. The service was first launched in the US in 2014.Gurman said Apple Pay is expected to support UPI alongside card payments. UPI is India's widely used digital payments system and allows users to make instant payments through participating banks and apps. However, Reuters' recent report about Apple's India plans did not mention UPI as part of the initial rollout.Earlier reports had also suggested that Apple Pay could initially launch without UPI, with support potentially added later.According to Reuters, Axis Bank is expected to be Apple's first major banking partner when Apple Pay launches in India. Apple is reportedly preparing to support Axis Bank credit cards initially. The company is also in discussions with HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank, although commercial agreements with those lenders had not been finalised, according to the report.Apple is expected to add more banks over time through separate agreements with lenders.Apple has reportedly been discussing its India plans with several major banks and payment networks for months. A Bloomberg report in February said Apple was in talks with Axis Bank, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank, as well as Visa and Mastercard. At the time, Apple Pay was expected to launch around the middle of 2026, but that timeline did not happen.If the latest October timeline is accurate, Apple Pay could soon enter India's established digital payments market, initially with limited banking support before expanding to more lenders.
Article Summary: Apple Pay could finally launch in India as early as October, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. Gurman said Apple is preparing to launch Apple Pay in India ‘finally’ next month. The service is expected to support card payments, while there are also reports that Apple could bring UPI support to the platform.

Article Title: Iran war risk: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warns of oil shocks, sticky inflation and higher interest rates
Article Text: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has warned that the ongoing war in Iran could trigger oil and commodity price shocks, keeping inflation elevated and pushing interest rates higher than current market expectations, Reuters reported.The warning came in his annual letter to shareholders, a day after US President Donald Trump escalated pressure on Iran by threatening to target key infrastructure if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened."Now, because of the war in Iran, we additionally face the potential for significant ongoing oil and commodity price shocks, along with the reshaping of global supply chains, which may lead to stickier inflation and ultimately higher interest rates than markets currently expect," Dimon said, news agency Reuters quoted as saying.Dimon, who has led JPMorgan for two decades, also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China."The challenges we all face are significant," he added.He said it remains uncertain whether the Iran war will achieve US objectives, while warning that nuclear proliferation remains the biggest risk linked to Iran.Markets have already begun pricing in these risks, with expectations of interest rate cuts this year largely fading amid rising inflation concerns triggered by the conflict.Last week, the benchmark S&P 500 index recorded its worst quarterly performance since 2022, weighed down by rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty since late February.Dimon noted that the US economy remains resilient, with consumers continuing to earn and spend, and businesses staying broadly healthy, though signs of weakening have emerged.He cautioned that economic strength has been supported by significant government deficit spending and past stimulus, while infrastructure investment needs continue to grow.At the same time, he pointed to positives such as fiscal stimulus under President Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill", deregulation policies and rising capital expenditure driven by artificial intelligence.On financial stability, Dimon said the $1.8-trillion private credit market "probably" does not pose a systemic risk, despite investor concerns and recent withdrawals from such funds.However, he warned that in a downturn, losses across leveraged lending could exceed expectations as credit standards have weakened.Private credit markets also lack transparency and rigorous valuation benchmarks, increasing the risk of investor exits if conditions worsen, he said.Separately, Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical" and "very flawed".He said JPMorgan’s GSIB surcharge would fall only to 5.0%, a level he described as “absurd” and “un-American”, arguing it penalises the bank’s scale and performance.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warns Iran war could trigger oil and commodity price shocks. He also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China. Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical"

Article Title: How selling Alaska in 1867 was a costly mistake for Russia
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

Why Russia agreed to the Alaska purchase

The hidden wealth Russia gave away

Strategic and geopolitical consequences

In 1867, Russia’s decision to sell Alaska to America turned out to be a historic mistake that was to go unnoticed for years to come. The sum paid by the US was only $7,200,000. Although, in the light of the circumstances at the time, it appeared logical, retrospectively, the act looks extremely shortsighted. Russia found itself economically constrained, geographically far away from the region and fearful of its falling into the hands of the British without any compensation. In reality, however, the region had proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Its vast reserves of oil, gold, and natural resources would later transform it into one of the most economically significant territories in the United States.The choice of selling Alaska was based on economic and political reasons. By the middle of the 19th century, the Russian Empire experienced financial difficulties as a result of the expensive Crimean War. It had become increasingly hard for the country to manage such remote and thinly populated areas as Alaska.According to EBSCO , “the Russian-American Company was in decline, and the colony failed to yield any profit”.In addition to this, the lucrative fur trade had declined, making the territory much less economically valuable for the empire.At the same time, Russia was afraid that Britain might capture Alaska in case another war broke out between the two countries. Selling the colony to the friendly United States appeared as a logical step. As the Office of the Historian states, William H. Seward, U.S. Secretary of State, “it was a chance to expand its influence in North America and hinder further growth of Britain”.For Russia, the transaction was a chance to minimise the losses. However, it greatly undervalued the potential of Alaska.Another thing that Russia did not expect was the amount of riches that Alaska possessed. Within several decades after the acquisition, the state saw discoveries of enormous deposits of gold, oil, and other minerals.“Alaska has produced more than 40 million ounces of gold,” according to the US Geological Survey. Furthermore, Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) . But even more importantly, the state's oil deposits turned out to be extremely valuable. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968 and became one of North America's biggest.In retrospect, the amount paid by the Americans, $7.2 million, or two cents per acre, was rather laughable. According to Howard I. Kushner , the deal “robbed Russia of an enormously rich territory, the true value of which would only be recognised in the twentieth century.”In addition to resources, there is the question of strategy and how important Alaska is to the United States from a strategic standpoint. This is a very good place when it comes to defence strategy. It borders on the Arctic Ocean and also happens to be close to Russia.During the period of the Cold War, the Alaskan region became a frontier area for the United States, becoming home to military facilities and warning systems.According to Col. Michael J. Forsyth, U.S. Army, the closeness of Russia and Alaska, only about ninety kilometres apart across the Bering Strait, meant that this region became highly significant to the United States' defence plans.From today's point of view, the strategic location of Alaska makes the state very important to the policies of the U.S. related to the Arctic, energy security, and even environmental policies.Thinking back, what seems clear to us now is that the Russians sold Alaska due to immediate needs rather than future considerations. In order to solve the problem, they lost a valuable resource for Russia.Conclusively, the Alaska Purchase should not have been done as it has had a significant impact that will remain throughout history.
Article Summary: Russia sold Alaska to the U.S. in 1867 for only $7,200,000. However, the region proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies

AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.

Article Title: From Delhi to other cities: Why unsafe buildings are becoming an urban time bomb
Article Text:
Many buildings across Indian cities are declared unsafe for habitation

Warning signs

Unsafe building warning

Noida reveals the cost of acting too late

Delhi's Sa​tya Niketan building collapse​

Problem spreading to older urban housing

Problem spreading across cities

Don’t wait for the next collapse

Don't wait for a collapse





NEW DELHI: The collapse of a five-storey paying guest accommodation in Delhi’s Satya Niketan killing seven people has once again brought the spotlight back on a danger that is lurking in plain sight in India’s fast growing cities.The tragedy had not been of one building, or one locality.All over India, old buildings, illegal additions, bad maintenance and changing uses of residential properties are creating a widening gap between where people live and how safely those buildings are being used.The crackdown in Delhi post-collapse exposes the scale of the problem. Between June 1 and September 9, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi took action on 1,053 properties for demolition, sealed 491 properties, and issued 2,316 show-cause notices and 757 notices for demolition.The civic body also surveyed 1,252 PG buildings between September 7 and 9, demonstrating the scale of the accommodation and enforcement challenge in the capital.But the worry is not confined to the borders of Delhi. More than 150 buildings in Ghaziabad have been declared unsafe or dangerous, compared to 26 in a 2018 survey and 102 in 2020.More than 500 people are still living in a dilapidated colony at Tulsi Niketan where there are 220 LIG flats, 2,004 EWS flats and 60 shops.The numbers demonstrate just how quickly a known structural problem can become a long-term habitation issue.Noida also throws up an uncomfortable question: what do you do when the authorities know that buildings are unsafe but people continue to live in them? After Satya Niketan fell, the Noida Authority started serving notices to vacate 56 buildings which it had declared years ago as dilapidated and unsafe.Following the Shahberi collapse in a 2018 survey, the authority identified 1,757 unauthorized structures including 56 dilapidated buildings.Evacuation alone is not the complete answer to safety for residents. Families need alternative accommodation, rehabilitation and a clear timeline for repair or redevelopment. This is all the more important in the case of older neighborhoods and economically weaker settlements, where residents have nowhere else to go.A building may stay occupied not because it is safe but because it is financially and practically impossible to leave.Other cities are under similar threats. The 2025 survey in Chennai identified 337 dilapidated structures including 130 buildings of the Greater Chennai Corporation.The civic body has now planned inspections ahead of the northeast monsoon and is seeking help from IIT-Madras, Anna University or PWD to check structural safety.Earlier this year, the civic body had declared over 500 buildings in Navi Mumbai as unsafe for living. As per the relevant Maharashtra provisions, buildings over 30 years old need to get structural audits done.Civic action in Mumbai itself has also tackled unauthorized alterations in high-rises, pointing to another facet of the problem: even relatively new buildings can pose safety risks if sanctioned plans are changed or common areas are repurposed without proper clearance.The bigger safety issue is stark in its size. The Times of India reported recently, citing government data, that nearly 33,000 people died in India in building collapses, fires and falls into pits and manholes between 2020 and 2024.The majority of these deaths occurred in urban areas, reflecting the effects of poor maintenance, enforcement and compliance of safety regulations.So the real challenge for the Indian cities is not only to identify unsafe buildings post-disaster. It is creating a system where structural audits are done on a regular basis, changes in building use are detected early, illegal construction is stopped before it becomes permanent and redevelopment does not get stuck for years.The collapse of Satya Niketan should not be viewed as an isolated incident but as a warning signal that the next urban disaster is already present in a street near us.
Article Summary: The collapse of a five-storey paying guest accommodation in Delhi’s Satya Niketan killing seven people has once again brought the spotlight back on a danger that is lurking in plain sight. Old buildings, illegal additions, bad maintenance and changing uses of residential properties are creating a widening gap between where people live and how safely those buildings are being used.

Article Title: Weather tomorrow: IMD forecasts rain, thunderstorms in several states; red alert in Odisha, Delhi-NCR likely to stay dry
Article Text:
(Representative image) Rain and thunderstorms are forecast across several Indian states in the coming days

Delhi-NCR weather

Kerala weather

Odisha weather

Andhra Pradesh weather

Bay of Bengal weather system

Latest IMD update





NEW DELHI: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast rain and thunderstorms across several states in the coming days, with heavy rainfall expected in parts of Kerala and Odisha, while no significant rainfall is expected in Delhi-NCR as the southwest monsoon continues to withdraw from parts of northwest India.Delhi, Noida, Gurugram, Ghaziabad and Faridabad are likely to remain largely dry on Tuesday, with no significant rainfall expected. The region is expected to remain largely dry over the coming days as the southwest monsoon withdraws from northwest India.The IMD has forecast light to moderate rainfall in several parts of Kerala from September 21 to 25, with isolated heavy rainfall likely in Pathanamthitta, Kottayam, Alappuzha, Ernakulam, Idukki and Thrissur.Residents in areas prone to waterlogging and landslides have been advised to remain alert and follow instructions from local authorities.Odisha is likely to receive heavy to extremely heavy rainfall under the influence of a deep depression over the Bay of Bengal.A red alert for extremely heavy rainfall of more than 20 cm has been issued for Kandhamal, Gajapati, Ganjam and Puri on September 23. Kalahandi, Kandhamal and Rayagada are under a similar red alert for September 24.Several other southern districts have been issued orange alerts for heavy to very heavy rainfall. The IMD has issued red, orange and yellow alerts for different districts until September 27.The South Odisha-North Andhra Pradesh coast is likely to experience squally conditions as the deep depression moves towards the coast.Winds of 55-65 kmph are likely along and off the coast from September 23 to the evening of September 24.The deep depression is expected to move towards the South Odisha-North Andhra Pradesh coast and reach the westcentral and adjoining northwest Bay of Bengal near the coast around the morning of September 23.Wind speeds could reach 75 kmph over the westcentral and adjoining northwest Bay of Bengal on September 23 and continue until the evening of September 24.The IMD has advised fishermen not to venture into the Andaman Sea until September 21, the eastcentral and adjoining northeast Bay of Bengal until September 22, and the westcentral and adjoining northwest Bay of Bengal and along the Andhra Pradesh-Odisha-West Bengal coasts from September 22 to 24.The southwest monsoon continues to withdraw from parts of northwest India, keeping Delhi-NCR largely dry. Meanwhile, rainfall activity is expected to remain active over parts of eastern and southern India in the coming days, particularly under the influence of the Bay of Bengal system.
Article Summary: IMD has forecast rain and thunderstorms across several Indian states in coming days. Heavy rainfall expected in parts of Kerala and Odisha, while no significant rainfall is expected in Delhi-NCR. The southwest monsoon continues to withdraw from parts of northwest India.

Article Title: New twist as fraud case, Rs 4-crore property row come under lens in Delhi executive Yuvraj Singh Manchanda's death
Article Text:
Investigators are examining financial dealings of Anya Vats and Sanyam Sachdeva





NEW DELHI: A Rs 1.2-crore cheating case and a separate dispute over a property worth around Rs 4 crore have come under the scanner in the probe into the killing of Delhi executive Yuvraj Singh Manchanda, with investigators examining whether he had learnt about the alleged financial dealings involving his former colleagues Anya Vats and Sanyam Sachdeva before his death.Police, however, are yet to establish any direct link between the two cases and Manchanda's alleged killing. Officials said the cases are being examined as part of the background of the accused and to understand the nature of their financial dealings.The cheating case was registered at Parliament Street police station in August following a complaint by a senior executive of a non-banking financial company, who was a former schoolmate of Sachdeva, a senior police officer said.According to the complaint, the executive was allegedly targeted from September 2024 and sent what was purported to be a notice from the Enforcement Directorate Sachdeva and Vats allegedly told him they had high-level government connections and could help settle the matter.They allegedly used fabricated notices purportedly issued in the name of the Union Home Ministry and referred to purported cases under laws including the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act and the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, the officer said.The complainant alleged that he transferred more than Rs 1.2 crore, primarily to Vats' bank account, arranging the money through his savings, loans and borrowings from family members.Vats allegedly later demanded another Rs 26 crore and claimed that Rs 13.8 crore had been paid to government agencies on the complainant's behalf.The FIR also mentions a message allegedly sent to the complainant in which he was pressured to repay the money before a deadline. The message read: "Sell your wife/do anything, just repay this."Investigators are now examining whether Manchanda knew about these alleged activities and whether this could have any connection with the circumstances leading to his death.Police are also looking into a separate dispute involving a property in Greater Noida valued at around Rs 4 crore and involving Sachdeva, his estranged wife and Vats.Sachdeva's estranged wife had also filed a domestic violence complaint, sources said.Manchanda, Vats and Sachdeva had earlier worked together at a real estate firm. Vats was subsequently removed from the company over alleged financial irregularities, according to police.Vats, who along with Sachdeva has been arrested in connection with Manchanda's alleged killing, has told investigators that she had given around Rs 1 crore to the executive and that the money had not been returned, sources said.Police are verifying the claim, the nature of the transaction and whether it was connected to any of the financial disputes or alleged irregularities being examined.According to investigators, the SUV allegedly used to transport Manchanda's body was taken to a residential society where Vats lived on September 6, the day he went missing.CCTV footage showed that the vehicle was moved out of the society the following day and parked at a facility near the residential complex, where it remained until September 8.The accused allegedly dumped Manchanda's body in a drain within the Badshahpur police station limits in Gurugram on September 8 and fled the city the following day, police said.Manchanda's body was recovered on September 10. His family has alleged that they were not informed about the recovery and that the unidentified body was cremated on September 14.Manchanda had gone to Gurugram on September 6 to meet Vats, a former colleague. Police have arrested Vats and Sachdeva in connection with his alleged killing. Investigators have been examining their movements and the circumstances surrounding his death.A post-mortem examination was conducted by Gurugram police.The force is expected to hand over its report and other documents related to the murder investigation to Delhi Police, officials said.The documents are expected to help investigators establish the cause of death and examine other forensic details.The details of how Manchanda was allegedly killed have not been officially disclosed.(With PTI inputs)
Article Summary: Police are yet to establish any direct link between the two cases and Manchanda's alleged killing. Officials said the cases are being examined as part of the background of the accused and to understand the nature of their financial dealings. Police are also looking into a separate dispute involving a property in Greater Noida.
